projects.title: COVID-Rx Chest X-ray Classification Prototype
projects.description: I built a research and application workflow for comparing ten CNN families on a public chest X-ray classification task, then exposed the selected experiments through both a PyQt desktop interface and a Flask web interface. The project combined dataset preparation, repeatable preprocessing, model comparison, probability outputs, and visual explanation.
projects.problem: Comparing image classifiers is not only a matter of choosing a larger network. Data sources, class balance, resize policy, normalization, model family, training configuration, evaluation metrics, and user-facing interpretation all affect what the comparison means. I needed a workflow that could register experiments and make model behavior inspectable without presenting it as a clinical diagnostic device.
contributions: Curated a comprehensive dataset of 36k+ chest X-ray images from multiple sources including 10,000+ COVID-19 cases, 15,000+ healthy cases, and 11,000+ pneumonia cases, ensuring robust model training.

Trained and benchmarked 10 state-of-the-art CNN architectures (VGG19, DenseNet, MobileNet, AlexNet, EfficientNet, InceptionV3, ResNet, RexNet, Inception-ResNet, Xception) achieving >90% accuracy in COVID-19 detection.
Developed dual-interface prototype: PyQt desktop application and Flask web application, enabling users to upload X-ray images and inspect model probabilities for the evaluated classes.

Implemented explainability features with heatmap visualizations showing image regions associated with model output, providing an inspection aid without claiming clinical decision support or diagnostic validity.

technicalDecisions.title: Separate comparison from clinical claims
technicalDecisions.text: A reported accuracy figure belongs to the project experiment and dataset context. It is not a clinical validation claim, deployment approval, or evidence that the system can replace a radiologist.

technicalDecisions.title: Use heatmaps as an inspection aid
technicalDecisions.text: CAM-family maps can reveal whether the model appears to use plausible image regions, but remain an interpretability aid and not a guarantee that the prediction is correct.

implementation.title: Make the data policy explicit
implementation.text: I treated the public sources, class composition, image dimensions, normalization, and dataset preparation as part of the experiment definition. A metric is meaningful only in the context of the data policy that produced it.

implementation.title: Compare model families under a shared interface
implementation.text: The project brought ten CNN families into one PyTorch application flow so architecture changes could be compared through the same prediction and presentation path.

implementation.title: Register metrics instead of relying on memory
implementation.text: Experiment tracking was part of the owner-reported workflow, including MLflow. I do not invent a leaderboard, split strategy, or exact metric table that is not present in the public source.

implementation.title: Connect inference to an inspectable interface
implementation.text: The desktop and web interfaces expose probabilities and heatmaps so a user can inspect the output instead of receiving an opaque class label.

architecture.summary: The system moved from a multi-class chest X-ray dataset through model-specific preprocessing and ten PyTorch CNN implementations into evaluation records, probability outputs, and CAM-family heatmaps. The public source is an implementation reference, not a complete clinical validation protocol.

projects.title: AbogacIA - AI Legal Platform
projects.description: I shaped AbogacIA as a domain-aware professional knowledge and writing assistant for Colombian legal work. It combines document ingestion, semantic retrieval, similar-case discovery, context-aware questions, and drafting support so a lawyer can work from relevant sources instead of starting from an empty page.
projects.problem: Legal work requires more than a generic chat response: the assistant needs to retrieve relevant sentences, codes, constitutional material, and regulations, then keep the user’s case context in view while suggesting sources or draft content. The system is an assistive workflow, not an autonomous legal decision-maker and not a guarantee of legal correctness.
contributions: Automatic Legal Document Analysis: When users upload case documents and descriptions, the system automatically identifies relevant regulations, rights, and specific articles that may be violated or related to the case.
Similar Case Recommendations: Provides lawyers with a comprehensive view of similar judicial sentences and precedents, helping them understand how similar cases were resolved in the past.
Intelligent Q&A System: Enables lawyers to ask questions about their case, recommended cases, or legal regulations, receiving accurate answers powered by RAG and LangGraph technology.
Document Generation: Allows construction of legal documents based on collected information, case analysis, and relevant regulations, streamlining the document creation process.

Advanced Database Architecture: Implemented vector database (Chroma) for semantic search and similarity matching, and graph database for complex legal relationships and precedent connections, enabling sophisticated legal document retrieval and analysis.

technicalDecisions.title: Use retrieval as evidence support
technicalDecisions.text: The architecture emphasizes potentially relevant source material and similar cases rather than implying that an LLM can independently determine the correct legal outcome.

technicalDecisions.title: Treat other domains as a direction
technicalDecisions.text: The retrieval-and-context pattern could be adapted to medicine or psychology in principle, but those extensions are conceptual and do not represent implemented or validated domain capabilities here.

implementation.title: Keep case context visible
implementation.text: Uploaded documents, user descriptions, questions, retrieved passages, and similar cases form the working context for the professional workflow.

implementation.title: Separate support from decision-making
implementation.text: The system helps research, compare, explain, and draft. A lawyer still reviews sources, interprets the law, and decides what belongs in a final document.

architecture.summary: The prototype combines public-source collection, document processing, vector retrieval in Chroma, graph-oriented relationship support, and LangGraph orchestration. Retrieved context feeds professional Q&A and drafting flows while the user remains responsible for reviewing the material.

projects.title: Industrial Computer Vision Systems
projects.description: I spent almost four years building computer-vision systems for industrial environments. One of the most important things I learned is that the model is only one part of a machine-vision system. Camera selection, optics, lighting, timing, and integration with the production line can matter just as much as the algorithm.
projects.problem: An inspection system has to make a useful decision from imperfect physical evidence and then fit into a moving production process. A defect may be smaller than the available pixels, reflections may change with the material or lighting, and a correct classification is still operationally useless if the trigger, PLC signal, operator interface, or reject mechanism is unreliable. The engineering problem was to design the complete path instead of treating inference as the product.
contributions: Developed and deployed real-time CV pipelines for defect detection, product fill checks, surface anomalies, and PPE compliance analytics, improving incident detection by 30% and reducing false alarms by 45%.
Built robust data/labeling workflows using CVAT, automated retraining, and OpenCV post-processing to meet factory latency/throughput constraints.
Architected imaging stacks (illumination, sensors, 3D scanners, thermal/LiDAR) and deployed an Optical Gas Imaging solution with PLC alarms, reducing time-to-detection of hazardous leaks.
Integrated CV modules with PLCs and C# HMIs to enable real-time defect rejection at production speed, complemented with a React-based console for live video overlays and dashboards.

technicalDecisions.title: Design the image before tuning the model
technicalDecisions.text: A higher-capacity model cannot recover information that the camera, lens, trigger, or lighting never captured. Improving the evidence often produced a more reliable system than adding algorithmic complexity.

technicalDecisions.title: Choose deterministic or learned processing deliberately
technicalDecisions.text: Classical computer vision was easier to inspect and maintain for explicit geometry; learned models were valuable when the variation was difficult to enumerate. The decision depended on data, explainability, maintenance, and the operating environment.

technicalDecisions.title: Set thresholds around operational consequences
technicalDecisions.text: A false negative and a false positive do not cost the same thing in every line. I treated operating thresholds as part of the system design, not just a model-training afterthought.

implementation.title: Start with the physical scene
implementation.text: I translated inspection requirements into imaging constraints: field of view, smallest defect, required resolution, working distance, focal length, depth of field, acquisition speed, and the likely sources of reflection or environmental variation. Camera and lighting cost mattered, but so did repeatability and serviceability on the factory floor.

implementation.title: Use deterministic vision when the structure is explicit
implementation.text: Filtering, contrast enhancement, thresholding, morphology, contour extraction, blob analysis, calibration, regions of interest, and geometric measurements were useful when the appearance and rule were stable. This kept the system understandable and avoided training a model for a problem that could be measured directly.

implementation.title: Build data and learned models when variation demands it
implementation.text: For changing product appearance, orientation, lighting, or background conditions, I worked with labeling workflows, CNN/YOLO-style training, error analysis, and operating thresholds. The right threshold depended on the cost of missing a defect versus stopping the line for a false alarm.

implementation.title: Integrate the decision into the line
implementation.text: The systems connected real-time acquisition and processing with operator interfaces, PLC/HMI communication, alarms, and rejection mechanisms. Desktop, C#, React, and lower-level integration choices varied with the installation rather than being prescribed as one universal stack.

implementation.title: Lead delivery across a portfolio of projects
implementation.text: I led a team of 10 engineers across more than 30 industrial computer-vision projects. The work ranged across defect detection, fill checks, surface anomalies, PPE compliance, and specialized imaging where the inspection required it.

architecture.summary: I worked from the physical scene toward the software decision: define the defect or safety requirement, select the acquisition setup, calibrate the image, choose deterministic processing or a learned model, validate behavior under production variation, and integrate the result with the operator and line controls. The exact stack varied by installation; not every project used every camera type, model family, or specialized sensor.

projects.title: Coding Agent Evaluation Workbench
projects.description: I built an internal, UI-driven workbench to compare coding-agent runs under reproducible conditions. Each evaluation starts with a shared reference task and prompts, records the selected tool, model and version, tester, date, scenario, model profile, and environment, then guides the evaluator through setup, execution, evidence collection, review, and export. The workbench is not an autonomous judge or a leaderboard; it preserves the evidence needed to explain a result later.
projects.problem: Comparing coding agents is harder than giving them the same prompt and checking which one finishes first. A run can produce convincing code while failing tests, ignoring a security constraint, or quietly changing the scope. I needed a way to hold the task and starting conditions steady, then reconstruct what happened months later instead of relying on a final screenshot or someone’s notes.

technicalDecisions.title: Hold the reference task steady
technicalDecisions.text: I used the same versioned task and prompts for comparable runs, then recorded any follow-up scenario rather than silently changing the task mid-experiment.

technicalDecisions.title: Keep automated signals separate from judgment
technicalDecisions.text: Build, test, lint, coverage, type, security, and authorization evidence stays distinct from rubric review. A passing test suite is useful evidence, not a complete measure of engineering quality.

technicalDecisions.title: Evidence before summary
technicalDecisions.text: I retained metadata, configuration, diffs, logs, transcripts, test results, rubric decisions, and reviewer notes before assembling a comparison. That makes it possible to challenge a conclusion instead of trusting a headline score.

technicalDecisions.title: Treat the LLM reviewer as advisory
technicalDecisions.text: An LLM can surface a bug or suggest a rubric interpretation, but the human evaluator remains responsible for the final assessment and for deciding whether the evidence supports it.

implementation.title: Separate repositories and experiment branches
implementation.text: I kept the benchmark/reference repository separate from the evaluation repository. Each experiment used its own Git branch so the reference task, generated patch, and run artifacts stayed tied to one reproducible setup.

implementation.title: Guided run setup
implementation.text: The UI captured the tool, model and version, tester, date, scenario, model profile, environment, shared reference task, and prompts before execution. The wizard made the process repeatable for someone who did not design the benchmark.

implementation.title: Execution and evidence capture
implementation.text: During a run I recorded elapsed time, interventions, self-corrections, questions, execution logs, the conversation transcript, configuration, code diffs, and resulting artifacts. That context matters when a run needs to be reconstructed later.

implementation.title: Objective verification
implementation.text: The evaluation ran code execution and CI checks for builds, linting, tests, coverage, type checks, and required constraints. These signals are repeatable, but they do not answer every architectural or security question.

implementation.title: Human and advisory review
implementation.text: A human evaluator reviewed architecture, maintainability, testing, documentation, security, and policy violations against anchored rubrics. An optional LLM reviewer could identify possible bugs, add notes, and suggest rubric scores, but I treated it as a second opinion rather than ground truth.

implementation.title: Export and comparison
implementation.text: The workbench exported an evidence bundle and structured experiment comparison so a conclusion could be traced back to the branch, prompt, transcript, code diff, CI result, rubric decision, and evaluator note.

architecture.summary: I kept the benchmark/reference repository separate from the evaluation repository. Each experiment received its own Git branch and run artifacts, while the workbench walked the evaluator through task specification, a clean checkout, agent execution, evidence capture, deterministic checks, rubric review, and export. That separation lets me inspect the exact generated code, patch, CI output, and transcript instead of treating the final result as a black box.

steps.description: Security and authorization reviews, structured human assessment, and model-assisted assessment where applicable add context.

limitations.text: Deterministic checks provide repeatable evidence but do not replace structured human or advisory assessment of security, authorization, and engineering quality.

technicalDecisions.title: Keep application and retrieval responsibilities distinct

technicalDecisions.title: Restrict high-risk capabilities by default
technicalDecisions.text: I treated application preview and code execution as bounded capabilities rather than as inevitable extensions of chat. The deeper execution design needed its own identity, session, workspace, and artifact controls.

technicalDecisions.title: Document the architecture at a safe abstraction level
technicalDecisions.text: I documented the useful engineering relationships at a level that can be shared: application, retrieval, persistence, integration, and authorization. Employer-owned topology, identifiers, private prompts, exact policies, and operational statistics remain out of scope.

projects.title: Policy-Governed AI Agents
projects.description: I worked on reusable foundations for conversational agents that could interact with operational systems without leaving authorization and failure handling to the language model. Each agent could have its own business workflow, but the platform needed a consistent way to interpret requests, resolve context, control state, execute tools, verify outcomes, and communicate safely. My contribution covered the relevant workflow and reliability workstreams, not an entire company platform.
projects.problem: Getting a language model to answer a question is one problem. Giving it the ability to act on someone’s behalf is another: it can misunderstand the request, select the wrong entity, skip a required confirmation, or describe a failed operation as successful. I needed the system—not a persuasive model response—to decide whether an action was allowed and whether it actually happened.

technicalDecisions.title: Deterministic transitions over unconstrained action selection
technicalDecisions.text: Explicit workflow states made the allowed progression visible and testable, while the language model remained responsible for interpretation rather than directly deciding that an operational action had completed.

technicalDecisions.title: Separate reasoning from operational execution
technicalDecisions.text: Keeping LLM reasoning distinct from structured tool execution created a control boundary for authorization, confirmation, result inspection, and escalation.

technicalDecisions.title: Verify before communicating success
technicalDecisions.text: A tool call or model-generated statement was not treated as proof of completion. The workflow required an observed, structured outcome before presenting supported success to the user.

technicalDecisions.title: Govern the response after execution
technicalDecisions.text: I treated routine responses, sensitive outcomes, adjudication or revision passes, refusals, degraded behavior, and escalation as separate response paths. Not every turn needed the same level of review, but every path needed explicit semantics.

technicalDecisions.title: Treat confirmation as conditional control
technicalDecisions.text: Confirmation was modeled as a boundary for applicable consequential actions rather than an indiscriminate interaction step, preserving usability without removing the control.

technicalDecisions.title: Use scenarios and traces to find failure modes
technicalDecisions.text: Scenario-based regression and trace inspection exposed negative, ambiguous, and state-transition failures more usefully than relying on aggregate scores or a single happy-path demonstration.

implementation.title: Stateful orchestration with LangGraph
implementation.text: I contributed to LangGraph-based workflow architecture with explicit states and controlled transitions, keeping the workflow understandable and testable rather than relying on unconstrained model-driven action selection.

implementation.title: Context and entity resolution
implementation.text: I implemented and refined the resolution of relevant context and entities before action paths could proceed, reducing ambiguity at the boundary between conversational interpretation and operational execution.

implementation.title: Authorization and verified actions
implementation.text: I worked on eligibility and policy checks, confirmation where required, authorized tool execution, structured outcomes, and verification before a success response was communicated.

implementation.title: Reliability improvements
implementation.text: I improved predictable handling for negative, ambiguous, failed, and incomplete paths, including clarification or escalation instead of silently treating an unverified operation as successful.

implementation.title: Multilingual response handling
implementation.text: I worked with English, Spanish, and French response handling while keeping action semantics, guardrails, and state transitions independent from the wording shown to the user. Where language coverage or rollout was incomplete, I treated that as a test boundary rather than assuming production parity.

implementation.title: Scenario-based evaluation and trace analysis
implementation.text: I contributed to scenario-based tests, regression coverage, state-transition validation, tool-result verification, trace inspection, and failure analysis without publishing internal datasets, counts, or production metrics.

implementation.title: Bounded engineering ownership
implementation.text: My ownership covered workflow architecture, implementation, reliability improvements, and evaluation within the relevant workstreams; I do not claim ownership of the entire employer AI platform.

architecture.summary: I separated the workflow into layers. An input-safety boundary assessed the request; model-assisted interpretation and entity resolution identified what the person meant; explicit state controlled what could happen next; deterministic business and authorization checks gated consequential actions; guarded tools returned structured outcomes; and response governance decided whether to answer, clarify, refuse, degrade, or escalate. The diagrams are generalized so they do not expose private workflow or policy details.

publicEvidence.text: I used scenario-based cases to exercise normal, negative, ambiguous, and failure paths without exposing the internal regression dataset or test counts.

publicEvidence.text: Workflow state and transition behavior were inspected as first-class reliability concerns, including whether a path could proceed, stop, clarify, or escalate.

publicEvidence.text: The evaluation approach distinguished a requested operation from an observed result so that a tool response or failure could be handled explicitly.

publicEvidence.title: Trace inspection and failure analysis
publicEvidence.text: Trace review helped identify interpretation, context, transition, execution, and verification failures without claiming a formal benchmark or universal coverage.

limitations.text: Stateful orchestration constrains progression but does not make language-model interpretation perfectly correct or deterministic.

limitations.text: The workflow can expose control points, but the quality and maintenance of eligibility criteria remain dependent on the surrounding business and operational context.

limitations.text: Incomplete, conflicting, or multilingual inputs may require clarification or escalation; this case does not claim a complete language or entity-coverage matrix.

limitations.title: Verification depends on observable outcomes
limitations.text: A workflow can verify only what its operational boundary exposes, so verification is not a guarantee that every downstream business effect is known.

limitations.title: No perfect safety or correctness claim
limitations.text: The approach reduces avoidable unsupported actions and makes failure paths more explicit; it does not claim zero failure risk, perfect policy compliance, or universal correctness.

projects.title: Professional Cases — AI-Powered Professional Practice Scenarios
projects.category: Independent AI Product Engineering / Knowledge Systems
projects.description: Professional Cases is an independent product under development for experienced and retired professionals who want to continue exercising professional judgment through realistic, profession-specific practice scenarios and respectful feedback. The verified repository contains a Next.js/React web surface, a FastAPI backend, knowledge and content tooling, case generation, semantic evaluation, and a partially integrated Senior runtime. The browser Senior experience still uses deterministic mock BFF routes, so this case does not present the product as launched or publicly available.
projects.problem: Professional knowledge arrives as heterogeneous documents, images, terminology, and domain context. Turning that material into useful practice requires more than retrieving a paragraph: the system needs traceable ingestion, searchable evidence, topic diversity, case seeds, generated narratives, quality checks, and feedback grounded in the professional work. The product goal is to preserve dignity and professional identity without reducing the experience to a generic quiz, an AI chatbot, or unsupported claims about learning outcomes.

technicalDecisions.title: Keep Admin/Content Studio separate from Senior UX
technicalDecisions.text: Knowledge authoring, clustering, generated-case review, and operations need dense inspection surfaces. The Senior experience needs a calm, readable, judgment-oriented flow; combining those surfaces would obscure both responsibilities.

technicalDecisions.title: Preserve provenance and safe projections
technicalDecisions.text: The backend stores evidence, runs, specifications, and internal evaluation data, but browser-facing projections are assembled field by field. Hidden answers, rubrics, prompts, evaluator confidence, and generation metadata are not treated as Senior-visible data.

technicalDecisions.title: Use hybrid retrieval with diversity controls
technicalDecisions.text: Lexical matching handles exact professional terms while vector search supports semantic recall. Per-document limits, clusters, and seed rotation reduce the risk that one source dominates every generated case.

technicalDecisions.title: Make the generation graph inspectable
technicalDecisions.text: Separate generation phases and persisted node runs make failure, quality judgments, image decisions, and refinement behavior visible to the content workflow instead of hiding everything behind one provider call.

technicalDecisions.title: Make scoring deterministic at the server boundary
technicalDecisions.text: The provider supplies constrained dimension judgments; the backend validates ids and evidence references and computes the weighted 1–100 result. This keeps scoring rules in an auditable contract rather than delegating the final number to the model.

technicalDecisions.title: Fail closed when authored content is incomplete
technicalDecisions.text: A missing evaluation specification or subject-knowledge contract is an explicit incomplete-content error. The system does not invent a generic rubric, patient reply, or fallback score to make the flow appear complete.

implementation.title: Modular product boundary
implementation.text: I worked across the Next.js/React web surface and the FastAPI/Python backend while keeping Admin/Content Studio concerns separate from the calmer Senior runtime. The repository uses explicit domain modules instead of collapsing knowledge, generation, evaluation, and runtime state into one client abstraction.

implementation.title: Evidence-grounded knowledge pipeline
implementation.text: I implemented and refined the path from supported document sources through extraction, Markdown-aware chunking, metadata, embeddings, image captions, pgvector persistence, hybrid retrieval, and related-image context. The pipeline exposes status and failure information instead of treating ingestion as an opaque batch.

implementation.title: Stateful case generation
implementation.text: I built the LangGraph generation path around material sufficiency, narrative generation, metadata extraction, image evaluation, quality judges, aggregation, optional refinement, finalization, and discard handling. Generated cases retain evidence references, quality metadata, node runs, and review state for Admin inspection.

implementation.title: Rubric and evaluation contracts
implementation.text: I separated the internal case-authored evaluation specification from provider output and the Senior-safe result. Evidence references are validated against the submitted work, the weighted overall score is assembled deterministically on the server, and malformed or hallucinated output does not receive a silent repair or fallback score.

implementation.title: Durable runtime foundations
implementation.text: I extended the backend runtime around assignment-owned state, authorization, idempotent conclusion submission, durable text messages, authored subject knowledge, finding persistence, leases, and explicit provider failure categories. Private notes and evaluator internals remain outside the evaluation input contract.

implementation.title: Bounded product claims
implementation.text: I kept voice, rewards, production browser cutover, and unverified multimedia capabilities outside the implemented claim set. The product remains independent and in development; no adoption, learning, clinical, or production-availability outcome is claimed.

architecture.summary: The current implementation is a modular web and backend monorepo. Admin and sponsor surfaces use Next.js/React; FastAPI modules own authentication, profiles, knowledge, generated cases, evaluation, and the Senior runtime; PostgreSQL with pgvector stores domain and retrieval data; Redis and Celery support background processing; and a centralized Google GenAI client forms the provider boundary. These diagrams show verified code paths, not the future deployment architecture or the full product design backlog.

publicEvidence.text: The repository includes unit coverage for knowledge metadata, clustering, case-generation nodes and service behavior, evaluation contracts and service behavior, case-subject contracts, provider errors, and seed rotation. publicEvidence.text: Integration suites cover authentication, knowledge upload and ingestion jobs, KB search, clustering, case-generation routes, evaluation persistence, Senior runtime authorization, and subject conversation behavior. They require the repository Docker Compose test database and were not run while that stack was stopped.

publicEvidence.title: Failure and security boundaries are tested
publicEvidence.text: The source and tests cover ownership checks, idempotency, provider failure, malformed structured output, hallucinated fact or evidence references, missing authored contracts, and the absence of private notes from provider inputs.

publicEvidence.title: Current validation finding
publicEvidence.text: The full unit run reached 140 passing tests but exposed one Windows locale failure while loading the UTF-8 patient_names.json file in a narrative-generator error-path test. That unrelated repository issue was not changed as part of this portfolio integration.

limitations.text: There is no public launch, adoption evidence, learning-improvement evidence, clinical effectiveness claim, or production availability claim in this case study.

limitations.title: Senior browser cutover is incomplete
limitations.text: The backend runtime and production conversation boundary exist, but the Next.js Senior BFF still uses deterministic mock routes. The current case therefore describes backend foundations and not a fully production-backed browser journey.

limitations.text: The conversation engine requires case-authored subject_knowledge_json, and semantic evaluation requires evaluation_spec_json. The current generation pipeline does not yet produce the subject contract, so not every generated case is conversable.

limitations.title: Voice and rewards are not delivered capabilities
limitations.text: Voice is explicitly deferred and no speech provider was found. Reward configuration exists at the profile level, but a reward ledger, event flow, and Senior presentation were not found.

limitations.title: Provider and environment boundaries
limitations.text: Provider-backed behavior depends on configured credentials and the Docker test stack. This portfolio case does not publish benchmark scores, user counts, latency, adoption, or other quality metrics.

projects.title: AI Digital Twin — Contextual Knowledge, GraphRAG & Retrieval Evaluation
projects.description: I became interested in the digital-twin problem through knowledge rather than avatars. A useful assistant would need to connect projects, people, dates, emails, meetings, and decisions, then recover the context behind a question instead of matching a few similar words. I focused on organizing contextual knowledge and comparing retrieval strategies; I am not presenting this as human-equivalent memory or as proof that every workplace integration is complete.
projects.problem: Professional knowledge is spread across documents, projects, dates, emails, meetings, and other records. Vector search is useful when the wording of a question differs from the source, but semantic similarity can miss who worked on a project, which meeting led to a decision, or how one event relates to another. I investigated whether graph-enhanced retrieval adds useful relationships over vector RAG, and what the quality and response-time trade-offs look like for different question types.

technicalDecisions.title: Compare retrieval strategies instead of assuming graph value
technicalDecisions.text: The central engineering question is empirical: determine when relationship-aware context adds value over vector similarity and where the additional complexity may not justify itself.

technicalDecisions.title: Use contextual metadata as part of retrieval reasoning
technicalDecisions.text: Projects, dates, source types, emails, and meetings provide context that can narrow or qualify a retrieval request. I leave the exact filter order and implementation unspecified.

technicalDecisions.title: Evaluate by question type
technicalDecisions.text: A single aggregate result could hide where vector, graph, or combined retrieval helps. I compared question types, but the specific categories and results remain private or unavailable.

technicalDecisions.title: Treat prompt changes as evaluation-driven
technicalDecisions.text: Prompt refinement is presented as a response to observed evaluation behavior, not as a claim that wording alone solved retrieval quality or latency trade-offs.

technicalDecisions.title: Do not imply automatic runtime routing
technicalDecisions.text: I describe comparable retrieval experiments, not an automatic router that selects a strategy for every question. That distinction remains until implementation evidence supports it.

implementation.title: Contextual knowledge organization
implementation.text: I organized the work around projects, dates, emails, meetings, and other context so retrieval could reflect more than semantic similarity alone. The exact schema, indexing code, and storage technology are not part of this public case.

implementation.title: Retrieval strategy experimentation
implementation.text: I compared vector RAG, GraphRAG, and a combined GraphRAG plus vector RAG strategy as retrieval engineering experiments.

implementation.title: Evaluation design
implementation.text: I compared the strategies across question types, measured response time, and assessed answer quality with DeepEval and an LLM-as-evaluator approach.

implementation.title: Prompt refinement
implementation.text: The experiments informed prompt improvements. I do not claim a particular score increase or universally superior retrieval strategy without the underlying artifacts.

architecture.summary: I organized the work around contextual records, metadata filters, and vector representations, then compared vector RAG, GraphRAG, and a combined approach before passing retrieved evidence to answer generation. I leave the exact database, graph persistence, extraction pipeline, fusion mechanism, session model, and runtime routing unspecified because those implementation artifacts were not available for this case.

projects.title: AI Agent Evaluation & Experimentation Framework
projects.description: I built a reusable evaluation platform for the question that follows any agent change: did the system improve, and where? The platform was designed to connect to a knowledge base through a small source contract, generate evaluation data from that source, run any compatible agent, and compare experiments with the same dataset and metric configuration. That made it possible to evaluate retrieval agents, tool-using agents, and multi-step workflows without coupling the runner to one implementation.
projects.problem: Manual testing makes it too easy to remember successful conversations and forget the awkward ones. Evaluation also becomes misleading when a dataset is built from one store while the agent searches another, or when every agent is forced into a response shape that hides retrieval and tool behavior. I needed a layer that preserved source context, normalized different agent outputs, and made the same experiment easy to repeat after a prompt, retrieval, model, or workflow change.

technicalDecisions.title: Make the knowledge-base boundary interchangeable
technicalDecisions.text: The builder should not care whether chunks come from a local vector store or an external knowledge base. A shared export-and-search contract keeps dataset creation and evaluation aligned while leaving the storage implementation replaceable.

technicalDecisions.title: Keep dataset methodology visible
technicalDecisions.text: Single-chunk, multi-chunk, and topic-based questions expose different failure modes. Recording the strategy, supporting chunks, source version, and retrieval context makes it possible to compare results without pretending every example measures the same behavior.

technicalDecisions.title: Use deterministic checks for hard contracts
technicalDecisions.text: Exact structured-output, action-trace, forbidden-action, invalid-parameter, and workflow-outcome checks are repeatable and easy to explain. They are the right tool when the contract is explicit, but they cannot judge every useful variation in a natural-language answer.

technicalDecisions.title: Compare metrics without hiding their assumptions
technicalDecisions.text: Reference-answer and semantic metrics help with meaning and groundedness, retrieval metrics need reliable context identities, and agent-specific metrics need traces or structured fields. I kept thresholds, weights, and metric inputs explicit so a comparison explains what was measured instead of collapsing everything into an unexplained score.

technicalDecisions.title: Make observability optional
technicalDecisions.text: The evaluation runner should still be useful without a live observability service. Optional tracing and experiment inspection make runs easier to investigate, but they are not a claim that every experiment was continuously monitored in production.

implementation.title: A knowledge-base boundary that stays interchangeable
implementation.text: I defined the dataset layer around a small source interface for bulk chunk retrieval and semantic search. That let the same builder use a local vector-store adapter or connect over HTTP to an external knowledge base, while keeping stable chunk identifiers and source metadata attached to each example. The practical requirement is explicit: a knowledge base must expose the fields needed for export and search; the evaluation logic itself is not tied to one vendor or storage engine.

implementation.title: Dataset generation through different methodologies
implementation.text: I supported three complementary ways to build evaluation data. Single-chunk generation creates focused baseline questions from one source chunk. Multi-chunk generation creates questions that require two to four chunks, grouped from the same document, adjacent sections, semantic neighbors, or precomputed clusters. Topic-based generation starts from realistic topic queries, retrieves relevant context, and asks the model to generate questions from that retrieved set. Each example keeps its supporting chunk IDs, answer context, source metadata, and generation method, so the dataset is inspectable rather than a bag of opaque prompts.

implementation.title: Any compatible agent can enter through the registry
implementation.text: Agents implement a common contract for running an input and reporting configuration. Registration keeps the experiment runner independent from the implementation, while the normalized output can carry the answer, retrieved IDs and text, tool calls, raw trace, latency, and metadata. The reference implementations cover deterministic RAG, tool-using ReAct, and supervisor-based multi-agent workflows; the same path can be extended with a custom agent adapter.

implementation.title: Metrics are registered by family and selected by contract
implementation.text: The metric registry made it possible to add and configure checks without changing the runner. The available families cover answer quality and grounding, retrieval ranking and recall, exact structured outputs, tool-call and workflow correctness, routing and escalation, safety and guardrails, runtime errors, latency, token usage, and response length. Thresholds and weights are explicit, and a metric is only meaningful when the selected agent exposes the evidence it needs.

implementation.title: Experiments that can be compared, not just executed
implementation.text: An experiment configuration selects the agent, dataset, metric definitions, thresholds, sample limits, and optional observability. Running the same dataset against different agent versions, prompts, retrieval strategies, or metric configurations produces JSON, CSV, and Markdown artifacts with per-example results, per-metric mean and pass-rate statistics, weighted summaries, timing, and failures. That makes it possible to compare experiments and metrics side by side without publishing private scores.

architecture.summary: I separated knowledge-base access, dataset preparation, agent execution, evidence capture, metric evaluation, and experiment analysis. A knowledge-base source provides bulk chunks and semantic search through one interface, so the builder can work with a local vector store or a compatible external knowledge base. Registered agents return a common output shape — answer, retrieved context, tool calls, trace, latency, and metadata — while the metric registry selects checks that match the evidence available for that experiment. Optional observability helps inspect runs; it is not the evaluation engine itself.

components.name: Knowledge-base source contract
components.role: Exposes bulk chunk retrieval and semantic search through the same interface for local vector stores or compatible external knowledge bases.

components.name: Dataset builder
components.role: Generates source-grounded examples with single-chunk, multi-chunk, and topic-based methodologies, including the supporting chunk identities and generation metadata.

components.name: Agent registry and adapters
components.role: Registers agent implementations behind a common run/configure interface, so RAG, ReAct, multi-agent, or custom agents can use the same runner.

components.name: Metric registry
components.role: Registers configurable metric implementations by type, threshold, weight, and the evidence fields an agent exposes.

components.name: Experiment runner
components.role: Runs fixed datasets, aggregates results, records errors and timing, and produces comparison-ready artifacts.

components.name: Optional Opik integration
components.role: Supports dataset, prompt, trace, and experiment inspection when configured; it is not presented as continuous production monitoring.

publicEvidence.title: Interchangeable source and registration boundaries
publicEvidence.text: The implementation separates knowledge-base adapters, dataset strategies, agent registration, metric registration, experiment execution, and observability. Those boundaries are testable independently and keep the runner from depending on one knowledge base or one agent architecture.

publicEvidence.title: Dataset and metric evidence
publicEvidence.text: Generated examples retain their supporting chunk identities, source metadata, strategy, and expected answer. Evaluation results retain configuration, outputs, timing, runtime failures, metric details, and comparison artifacts, which makes a failure inspectable rather than hidden behind a single average.

publicEvidence.title: Experiment comparison
publicEvidence.text: Run artifacts are structured for comparison across agent, prompt, retrieval, and metric configuration changes. I am intentionally not publishing private scores, rankings, benchmark results, or internal dataset examples.

limitations.title: Knowledge-base compatibility is explicit
limitations.text: The platform can work with different knowledge bases through the shared source contract, but a source still needs reliable bulk export, semantic search, stable chunk identities, and the metadata required by the selected metrics.

limitations.title: Generated datasets still need review
limitations.text: Synthetic generation improves coverage but does not remove the need for spot checks. Simple word-overlap validation is not sufficient for every multi-chunk answer, so dataset quality remains part of the evaluation design.

limitations.title: Metrics are contract-dependent
limitations.text: Not every agent exposes retrieved context, action traces, workflow outcomes, or reference fields. A metric should be applied only when its inputs and semantics are valid for that experiment.

limitations.title: Model-assisted assessment varies
limitations.text: LLM-based judges and semantic metrics introduce evaluator-model and prompt sensitivity. They complement deterministic checks; they do not remove the need for failure inspection or human judgment.

limitations.title: No public benchmark claim
limitations.text: The public case excludes private prompts, datasets, scores, rankings, model comparisons, and customer results. It documents the evaluation capability and design decisions rather than a headline improvement.

limitations.title: No continuous-monitoring claim
limitations.text: Opik integration supports optional tracing and experiment inspection; it does not by itself establish a continuously monitored production system.

projects.title: Secure AI Code Execution & Workspace Isolation
projects.description: Adding code execution to an AI workspace sounds straightforward until the code is not trusted. I approached the problem from identity and workspace boundaries first: how do I know which user owns a session, what files that session should see, whether the intended workspace is actually mounted, and what artifacts can safely return to the application?
projects.problem: Code execution creates a different trust boundary from text generation. A request can be authenticated and still be routed to the wrong workspace, attached to an unexpected filesystem, or allowed to survive longer than intended. I needed the execution path to verify ownership and runtime state before allowing a managed interpreter session to work with persistent files.

technicalDecisions.title: Reject caller-supplied workspace identity
technicalDecisions.text: Trusting a workspace ID in the request would make the most important authorization decision part of the user input. Deriving ownership from verified identity gives the gateway one authoritative starting point.

technicalDecisions.title: Separate execution from the chat application
technicalDecisions.text: A dedicated execution service makes runtime, filesystem, session, and artifact controls visible as their own boundary. It also avoids making the conversational application responsible for arbitrary interpreter lifecycle details.

technicalDecisions.title: Separate AgentCore execution from Sandpack previews
technicalDecisions.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter is the server-side code-execution path. Sandpack is the preview path for generated React or artifact output, protected by a separate HTTP authorization sidecar. Treating the two as the same sandbox would overstate what either boundary proves.

technicalDecisions.title: Persist workspaces, keep sessions ephemeral
technicalDecisions.text: Persistent owner-scoped storage supports useful files and artifacts, while managed interpreter sessions can remain short-lived. The trade-off is that the attachment and cleanup lifecycle must be verified instead of assumed.

technicalDecisions.title: Fail closed on unexpected runtime state
technicalDecisions.text: If the session, mount, or filesystem state does not match the authorized request, the safer behavior is to deny execution and surface a controlled failure rather than guessing which workspace was intended.

technicalDecisions.title: Be honest about the shared-role boundary
technicalDecisions.text: The design reduces accidental cross-owner access and incorrect routing at the application boundary. A shared interpreter resource and shared execution role are not a strong security boundary against mutually hostile users who can abuse those credentials, so I describe this as a controlled internal design rather than a hostile-tenant sandbox.

implementation.title: Integrate the CodeAPI Translator with AgentCore
implementation.text: I implemented and tested a TypeScript/Fastify CodeAPI adapter for AWS Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter. The translator is the application-facing boundary: it verifies identity and prepares the execution request, while AgentCore is the managed service that actually runs the code.

implementation.title: Derive ownership from authenticated identity
implementation.text: I kept workspace ownership on the server side. The execution request does not get to nominate an arbitrary workspace identity; the CodeAPI Translator resolves the owner from verified authentication context and uses that result for the rest of the flow.

implementation.title: Bind sessions to workspaces
implementation.text: I treated session creation and storage attachment as one relationship to verify. Before execution, the path checks that the intended owner-scoped access point is present and that the session state matches what the application authorized.

implementation.title: Harden filesystem and lifecycle behavior
implementation.text: The implementation includes bounded filesystem operations, storage restrictions, session lifecycle handling, EFS access-point checks, and validation that rejects unexpected mounts or session states rather than attempting to recover silently.

implementation.title: Keep file and artifact handling explicit
implementation.text: Uploads, downloads, and generated artifacts remain part of the security boundary. The execution service should return only artifacts associated with the verified workspace and expected session flow.

implementation.title: Keep artifact previews separate from code execution
implementation.text: The Sandpack preview path is a different capability: an ECS/Fargate-hosted bundler sits behind an HTTP authorization sidecar for generated React and artifact previews. That sidecar protects preview requests; it is not the AgentCore Code Interpreter and does not provide general-purpose hostile-code sandboxing.

implementation.title: Prepare infrastructure and security tests
implementation.text: I worked with infrastructure-as-code preparation and automated security-oriented tests for ownership and filesystem behavior. The implementation work is documented separately from staging activation and broader user routing.

architecture.summary: I separated the authenticated application from a TypeScript/Fastify CodeAPI Translator and the managed execution service. The translator verifies JWT-derived ownership, resolves the owner-bound EFS access point, checks session and mount state, and then invokes AWS Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter. AgentCore runs the code; EFS persists owner-scoped files; the translator owns the application-level session, filesystem, upload, download, and artifact checks. The shared interpreter resource and execution role remain an operational choice with a residual security limitation, not a complete hostile-tenant isolation boundary.

components.name: Authenticated translation/API layer
components.role: Receives the application request and passes verified identity context into the execution path.

components.name: TypeScript CodeAPI Translator
components.role: Resolves the owner and intended workspace server-side, validates the request, and invokes AgentCore instead of trusting a caller-supplied workspace identity.

components.name: AWS Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter
components.role: Runs the submitted code in managed interpreter sessions. AgentCore is the execution service; it is not the ECS-hosted translator.

components.name: Owner-scoped EFS workspace
components.role: Provides dynamically resolved per-owner access points for files that must persist across short-lived sessions.

components.name: Validation and artifact boundary
components.role: Checks session, mount, filesystem, upload, download, and artifact expectations before allowing or returning work.

publicEvidence.title: Source-level implementation
publicEvidence.text: The documented source components include the TypeScript/Fastify CodeAPI adapter for AgentCore, owner-bound EFS workspace resolution, session and mount checks, and automated tests for the ownership, filesystem, and artifact boundaries described here. The public case omits private resource names, policies, paths, credentials, and topology.

publicEvidence.title: Security-oriented test coverage
publicEvidence.text: I exercised the cases that matter when identity and runtime state disagree: incorrect ownership, unexpected filesystem access, invalid mounts, and unsafe session conditions should be rejected rather than allowed to drift into execution.

publicEvidence.title: Rollout status
publicEvidence.text: The source-level components and automated tests were reported complete, and the infrastructure configuration was reviewed. The handover did not confirm complete staging activation, full end-to-end rollout, or production deployment of the multi-owner architecture.

limitations.title: AgentCore, translator, and storage are separate components
limitations.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter runs code, the translator mediates application requests, and EFS persists workspaces. ECS/Fargate hosts the translator; it is not accurate to describe AgentCore itself as an ECS service or to treat EFS as the execution sandbox.

limitations.title: Sandpack is an artifact-preview boundary
limitations.text: The Sandpack bundler and HTTP authorization sidecar support generated artifact previews. They are not the same implementation as AgentCore Code Interpreter and are not presented as a general-purpose hostile-code sandbox.

limitations.title: Not a hostile-tenant isolation claim
limitations.text: A shared managed interpreter resource and associated shared execution role can still expose residual risk to mutually hostile users who can abuse those credentials. Application-level ownership checks reduce routing mistakes; they do not remove that threat model.

limitations.title: Controlled internal scope
limitations.text: The selected architecture was designed for a controlled internal environment. I do not describe it as unrestricted secure execution, a zero-trust sandbox, or a production-grade multitenancy guarantee.

limitations.title: Activation remained gated
limitations.text: Implementation and tests are not the same as a completed rollout. Broader routing, staging activation, acceptance, and production deployment required separate operational gates that were not confirmed in the available handover context.

limitations.title: Private infrastructure details stay private
limitations.text: The published case intentionally excludes IAM policies, resource identifiers, filesystem paths, endpoints, account structure, credentials, and proprietary threat-model details.

projects.title: Industrial Machine Vision — Course & Practical Labs
projects.description: I co-designed and delivered a public industrial machine-vision course with practical material that moves from pixels and image operators to cameras, optics, lighting, factory communication, and learned models. The repository is a collaborative teaching artifact: its value is the learning path and hands-on material, not an individual authorship claim.
projects.problem: Machine vision is often taught as either image processing or model training, while real systems require both technical layers plus physical imaging and industrial integration. The course connects those layers so a learner can understand why field of view, lens choice, illumination, calibration, feature design, dataset construction, and communication all affect the final inspection behavior.
contributions: Digital image processing: pixels, RGB and bit depth, filtering, edges, brightness and contrast, histograms, binarization, morphology, connected components, and shape or texture features.

Dimensioning systems: cameras, lenses, optics, field of view, resolution, depth of field, lighting, polarization, filters, thermography, optical gas imaging, 3D, hyperspectral and multispectral approaches.
Industrial integration: PC and smart cameras, FPGA and memory considerations, Ethernet/TCP/IP/PROFINET, and practical machine-vision communication exercises.
Machine and deep learning: feature-based classification, dataset construction, classical ML, neural networks, PyTorch, CNNs, evaluation, labs, and a final project.

technicalDecisions.title: Teach the system, not only the model
technicalDecisions.text: The course keeps physical image formation, deterministic processing, industrial communication, and learned inference in one progression so the model is understood as one component of a larger system.

technicalDecisions.title: Preserve collaborative authorship
technicalDecisions.text: I describe the course as co-designed and collaboratively delivered. The public repository is linked as the source of the modules, notebooks, slides, and labs rather than presented as an exclusively authored work.

implementation.title: Digital image processing
implementation.text: The first module builds from pixel representation and basic transformations through filtering, histograms, thresholding, morphology, connected components, and feature extraction such as size, curvature, circularity, perimeter, bounding boxes, centroids, texture, and moments.

implementation.title: Physical vision-system design
implementation.text: The material treats cameras, CCD/CMOS sensors, lenses, field of view, resolution, depth of field, illumination, polarization, filters, thermography, optical gas imaging, 3D, hyperspectral, multispectral, and stereo methods as system-design choices.

implementation.title: Practical industrial labs
implementation.text: The repository includes practical material around visible-camera and illumination setups, thermography, Gocator 3D work, Cognex smart-camera work, and industrial communication concepts.

implementation.title: Applied machine learning
implementation.text: Dataset construction, feature-based prediction and classification, basic ML, neural networks, PyTorch notebooks, CNNs, evaluation, and a final project complete the path.

architecture.summary: The learning path starts with digital images and deterministic operators, then introduces physical imaging systems, specialized sensors and lighting, industrial communication, and machine/deep learning. Labs and a final project connect each concept to an applied workflow.

workflow.title: A learning path from pixels to inspection systems
workflow.summary: Each stage adds a new engineering constraint while keeping the previous layer visible.

steps.title: Represent and transform the image
steps.description: Work with pixel matrices, color, bit depth, filtering, histograms, thresholding, edges, and morphology before choosing a model.

steps.title: Measure and extract structure
steps.description: Use connected components, contours, geometric measurements, texture, moments, and fitted curves to describe objects and defects.

steps.title: Design the physical imaging system
steps.description: Relate cameras, lenses, field of view, resolution, depth of field, lighting, polarization, filters, thermography, and 3D or smart-camera options to the inspection requirement.

steps.title: Connect the inspection to industry
steps.description: Explore industrial computers, camera platforms, Ethernet/TCP/IP/PROFINET, and practical communication or acquisition labs.

steps.title: Build and evaluate learned models
steps.description: Construct datasets, introduce classical ML and neural networks, use PyTorch and CNNs, and consolidate the work in a final project.

components.name: Image-processing foundations
components.role: Filtering, histograms, thresholding, morphology, features, and measurements provide a deterministic vocabulary for visual evidence.

components.name: Optics and acquisition
components.role: Cameras, lenses, field of view, resolution, depth of field, and lighting connect the physical scene to pixels.

components.name: Industrial imaging
components.role: Thermography, optical gas imaging, 3D, smart cameras, and communication labs show how specialized systems fit production constraints.

components.name: Machine and deep learning
components.role: Dataset construction, classical ML, PyTorch, neural networks, CNNs, and evaluation extend the toolkit when explicit rules are insufficient.

limitations.text: The labs and examples teach transferable concepts. They do not by themselves establish a production-ready inspection system, sensor specification, or industrial performance result.
